claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has an inherent, non-uniform native oxide film.
Chemical or electrochemical cleaning can remove the native oxide layer from Q235 steel.
Controlled re-oxidation can form a uniform, passivating oxide layer on Q235 steel.
The native oxide on untreated Q235 steel is patchy in morphology or composition.
An irregular oxide layer creates localized anodic and cathodic sites on untreated Q235 steel.
These localized electrochemical sites accelerate corrosion initiation and can promote pitting.
A uniform passivating oxide acts as a barrier to corrosive species, particularly chloride ions.
A uniform passivating oxide minimizes the formation of localized electrochemical cells.
Suppressing localized electrochemical cells slows corrosion initiation and propagation.
Q235 specimens with a uniform passivating oxide will show delayed corrosion onset relative to untreated specimens.
Q235 specimens with a uniform passivating oxide will have a lower corrosion rate than untreated specimens.
The predicted corrosion suppression will occur under both room-temperature and 60–80°C exposure conditions.
The proposed effect applies under moderate chloride concentration, humidity, and temperature conditions where additional temperature-driven degradation mechanisms do not dominate.
The engineered oxide layer may not remain stable during long-term cyclic environmental exposure.
A statistically significant delay in onset and at least a 20% corrosion-rate reduction under both tested temperatures would distinguish the predicted response from the untreated reference.
